Article.ArticleTitle: Mother's level of confidence in caring for her late preterm infant: A mixed methods study.

Abstract.AbstractText: To examine what it means to be a mother of a late preterm infant including a mother's level of confidence in caring for her late preterm infant over time and the effect of maternal depression of this experience.

Little is known about mothers' experiences of caring for their late preterm infants in the community, including their level of confidence and parenting stress within the context of a supported care environment by public health nurses.
A mixed methods study, sequential explanatory quantitative and qualitative study.

A convenience sample of mothers with late preterm infants (n = 71) completed questionnaires on maternal confidence (3 to 4 weeks, and 6 to 8 weeks), parenting stress (6 to 8 weeks), social support (6 to 8 weeks) and postpartum depression (6 to 8 weeks). A purposive sample of mothers (n = 11) underwent in-depth, semi-structured interviews.

Maternal confidence decreased from 3-4 weeks to 6-8 weeks after delivery and similar results were found for mothers who reported depressive symptoms. Narratives of the mothers suggested the decrease in maternal confidence over time was influenced by the demanding characteristics of the late preterm infant, the prospect of their re-hospitalization, and the mother's reported interactions with public health nurses. Depression had an effect on maternal confidence; that is, the depressed mothers demonstrated less confidence about their caretaking role than the non-depressed mothers at 6-8 weeks. Mothers did not discuss mental health issues, which may reflect the protective effects of social support on emotional instability or an inability to recognize postpartum depression.

The confidence of mothers with late preterm infants decreased over the first 2 months following delivery and being home with their infants. Assisting mothers to meet their personal needs and the needs of their infant should promote maternal skills, which will likely increase maternal confidence related to the care of their late preterm infant.
